477.title: Mudgala turns down heaven

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, Vyasa tells Yudhishthira about a sage named Mudgala, who is poor on purpose. He lives by gleaning, picking up the grain left in the fields after harvest, and every two weeks he cooks what he's gathered and feeds whoever comes to his door. Then the famously short-tempered sage Durvasa starts showing up, again and again, eating every last grain and smearing the leftovers on himself. Mudgala goes hungry, and never once gets angry. So heaven sends a chariot for him. A divine messenger at the door: get in.
screen: `A SAGE WHO LIVES ON GLEANINGS.` → `DURVASA EATS IT ALL.` → `A CHARIOT FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Mudgala doesn't get in. First he asks: what's heaven like, and what's wrong with it? The messenger is honest. Heaven is lovely: no hunger, no age, music, fine company. But there you only enjoy what you've already earned; you can't do any new good. You see others shining brighter than you. And when your merit runs out, you fall. So Mudgala sends the chariot away and turns to meditation, toward a place with no grief and no falling, and the story says he reached it. Here's the Hindu teaching, plainly. Heaven, svarga, is real, but it isn't the goal. It's a reward, and rewards run out. Krishna says it in the Gita: people enjoy the wide world of heaven, and when their merit is spent, they come back. The goal is moksha, freedom, which doesn't run out. Patanjali says it in yoga's terms. Sutra 3.49: full discernment brings knowing everything. Sutra 3.50: let go even of that, and freedom comes. Sutra 3.51: when those in high places invite you, don't cling and don't be proud, or the old trouble comes back. The classical commentary acts it out: gods arrive with chariots and an elixir against age, and the yogi says no. Notice the danger is the good stuff. Nobody needs a warning against misery. It's why Prahlada, offered any boon he liked, said that serving God for a reward makes you a trader, not a devotee. A Hindu can be glad of good things, a prize, praise, a raise, and still say: that isn't the point.
screen: `MUDGALA ASKS: WHAT'S WRONG WITH HEAVEN?` · `MERIT RUNS OUT. YOU FALL.` · `SVARGA IS A STOP. MOKSHA IS THE GOAL.` · `3.51: NO CLINGING, NO PRIDE.` · then, large: `HEAVEN ISN'T THE GOAL; FREEDOM IS.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath until something pleasant invites you away: a daydream, a plan, a drowsy warmth. Treat it like Mudgala's chariot. Notice it, thank it, don't get in. If you pray, let a name of God be how you come back: Ram, Krishna, Om namah Shivaya. If you don't, just come back to the breath. And if a little pride follows at having stayed, send that chariot away too.
Omniscience. Knowing everything, which Patanjali says comes from full discernment, and which he says to set down too, the way Mudgala set down heaven.

478.howItsDone: Hindus describe time as vast and cyclical, with yugas and days of Brahma, and many pray with a japa mala of 108 beads, one name at a time; students of the Yoga Sutras read 3.52–3.54 with the commentary's account of the instant.

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, a king named Kakudmi has a daughter, Revati, and he can't find anyone good enough for her. So he does what only a king of old could do. He takes her up to Brahma's own world, to ask the creator himself. When they arrive, Brahma is listening to the heavenly musicians, so father and daughter wait politely until the song ends. Then Kakudmi bows and reads out his list of possible husbands. And Brahma laughs.
screen: `A KING, A DAUGHTER, A LIST.` → `THEY WAIT FOR ONE SONG.` → `BRAHMA LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: Every man on your list, Brahma says, is gone, and their sons, and their grandsons, and their whole lines. While you waited for one song, twenty-seven great cycles of ages passed on earth. Go back and give her to Balarama, Krishna's brother. Kakudmi comes home to a changed world and does just that. Here's the teaching behind the joke. Hindus see time as vast, and turning. Four ages, the yugas, make one great cycle, and the Gita says a day of Brahma lasts a thousand yugas, which teachers read as a thousand of those great cycles; then a night, then a new creation. Not a line from start to finish, but a wheel. Time itself, Kala, is a face of God: in the Gita, Krishna says, I am time. Then Patanjali adds something startling. Sutra 3.52: rest samyama on the instant and its sequence, and discerning knowledge is born. The classical commentary says the instant, kshana, is the smallest piece of time, as the atom is of matter, and that hours, days and ages are put together by the mind. Only one instant is real at a time. Brahma's day and Kakudmi's song are both made of instants. Sutra 3.54 names the knowledge that sees this: taraka, the one that carries across, like a ferry over the river of becoming. So the two ideas meet. Time is huge, a wheel of ages, and you only ever live one instant of it. A Hindu can hold a cosmos billions of years old and this one breath in the same hand.
screen: `TWENTY-SEVEN GREAT CYCLES, ONE SONG.` · `FOUR YUGAS, ONE CYCLE.` · `A THOUSAND CYCLES, ONE DAY OF BRAHMA.` · `KSHANA: THE SMALLEST PIECE OF TIME.` · `TARAKA: THE ONE THAT CARRIES ACROSS.` · then, large: `TIME IS A WHEEL OF AGES, LIVED ONE INSTANT AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus pray with a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads, one name of God for each bead. Today let each bead, or each breath if you don't have one, be one instant: this touch of air, this name, then the next. When the mind builds something bigger, the rest of the week, the rest of the year, notice the building, and come back to this single bead.
Taraka, the knowledge that carries across, like a ferry over a river. It comes from seeing the instant clearly, and Hindu prayers use the same picture: crossing the ocean of becoming.

479.howItsDone: Hindus often describe puja, fasting, chanting and service as chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind, while the self (atman) is held to be already pure; many begin worship with water as a sign of purification, and teachers stress that kaivalya does not depend on any powers.

segments.voice: Shuka, son of the great sage Vyasa, is young, and he's leaving home for good, wandering with nothing, not even clothes. His father follows, calling after him. On the way they pass a pool where celestial women, apsaras, are bathing. Shuka walks right past, and the women don't move. A moment later old Vyasa comes by, fully dressed, and they hurry to cover themselves. Vyasa stops, puzzled. Why for me, and not for him?
screen: `SHUKA WALKS PAST. NOBODY MOVES.` → `VYASA WALKS PAST. THEY COVER UP.` → `WHY?`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives their answer in one line. You still see man and woman. Your son's sight is pure. Shuka wasn't stronger than his father; Vyasa is among the greatest sages there are. Shuka's mind simply added nothing of its own to what he saw, and everyone at that pool could feel the difference. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath. The self, the atman, is already pure. It was never stained, and Vedanta teachers often call it ever-pure. What gets cloudy is the mind. So Hindus speak of chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind, and say that's what puja, fasting, chanting and service are for. They don't wash the self. They wipe the glass. Patanjali ends his third book right there. Sutra 3.55: when the purity of the mind's clearest part, sattva, equals the purity of the seer, kaivalya. Freedom. Kaivalya comes from kevala: alone, whole, standing on its own. And the classical commentary adds a line that clears the table after weeks of strange powers: this freedom comes whether or not someone has the powers. Invisibility, strength, knowing other minds, the gods at the door: none of it was required. A mind like clean glass is. Shuka didn't fly or vanish at that pool. He just saw, without adding anything, and that was the whole difference. Book three is done.
screen: `YOUR SON'S SIGHT IS PURE.` · `ATMAN: ALREADY PURE.` · `CHITTA-SHUDDHI: CLEARING THE MIND.` · `3.55: WHEN THE TWO PURITIES ARE EQUAL.` · `WITH OR WITHOUT THE POWERS.` · then, large: `THE SELF IS PURE; PRACTICE CLEARS THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Many families begin puja by sprinkling a few drops of water and remembering God as the one who makes things pure. If you pray, begin that way. If you don't, rinse your hands slowly. Then rest on the breath and notice what the mind is adding right now: a mood, a judgment, a story about how this is going. Don't scrub. Let it settle, like silt in a glass of water, and look through again.
Kaivalya: freedom, from kevala, alone and whole. When the mind is as clear as the seer, the seer stands free, with or without any powers.

480.howItsDone: Hindus honor tapas but judge holiness by character: teachers point to the Gita's divine qualities (16.1–3) and its warning against self-torturing, ego-driven austerity (17.5–6), and read Yoga Sutra 4.1 as a reminder that powers come from many sources.

segments.voice: Book four of the Yoga Sutras, the last, opens with where powers come from, and the Bhagavata Purana has a story that makes its point. An asura named Vrika asks the sage Narada: which god is quickest to please? Shiva, says Narada. He gives fast, and he angers fast. So Vrika goes to Kedara, builds a fire, and starts cutting pieces of his own flesh and offering them in. Day after day. At last he raises the blade to his own head, and Shiva rises out of the fire and stops his hand. Ask, says Shiva.
screen: `WHICH GOD IS QUICKEST TO PLEASE?` → `A FIRE AT KEDARA.` → `ASK, SAYS SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Vrika asks: let whoever's head I touch, die. Shiva grants it, and Vrika reaches straight for Shiva's head. Shiva runs, to the ends of the earth, with Vrika chasing, until Vishnu steps in, disguised as a young student. Politely he asks: you trust that boon? Test it first. On yourself. Vrika touches his own head, and falls. The story is half a joke and all a warning. Sutra 4.1: powers are born of birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi. Five sources, and only one is samadhi. Tapas, fierce discipline, works for an asura too, so a power proves nothing about the person holding it. The Gita says it more sharply. Austerities that are terrible and self-torturing, done out of ego, craving and force, it calls asuric, demonic. Then it gives the real measure of a holy person, the divine qualities, daivi sampat: fearlessness, purity of heart, generosity, self-control, truthfulness, non-harming, freedom from anger, compassion, gentleness, modesty. That's the Hindu test. Not what someone can do, but what they're like. Vrika had a power that could kill a god, and none of the list. A grandmother who is patient with everyone and never makes a show of her prayers may have the whole list and no powers at all. The tradition knows which one it bows to.
screen: `LET WHOEVER'S HEAD I TOUCH, DIE.` · `4.1: FIVE SOURCES OF POWER.` · `SELF-TORTURE IS ASURIC.` · `DAIVI SAMPAT: THE DIVINE QUALITIES.` · then, large: `POWER ISN'T HOLINESS; CHARACTER IS.`

segments.voice: Shiva has a name for being easy to please: Ashutosh. Vrika used it to bargain. Today, if you pray, say Om namah Shivaya a few times and ask for nothing at all. If you don't, bring to mind one person whose gentleness you trust, and rest there. Then pick one quality from the Gita's list, patience, gentleness, truthfulness, and carry it through the day.
Kaivalya, freedom, the name of the Yoga Sutras' fourth book. It opens by naming five sources of power, birth, herbs, mantra, discipline and samadhi, so that no power gets mistaken for freedom.

segments.voice: The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras names two stories together. The first is Nahusha, a good human king, made king of heaven while Indra is in hiding. The throne goes to his head. He makes the great sages carry his litter like servants, and when the sage Agastya is too slow, Nahusha strikes him with his foot. Agastya says: fall, and be a snake. And the king of heaven drops to earth as a python. The second is Nandi, a human boy who loved Shiva so wholly that he became Shiva's own.
screen: `A KING OF HEAVEN KICKS A SAGE.` → `FALL, AND BE A SNAKE.` → `A BOY BECOMES SHIVA'S OWN.`

segments.voice: One went down, one went up, and Patanjali says it's the same law. Sutra 4.2: the change into another kind of being comes from nature overflowing. Sutra 4.3: your deeds don't set nature moving; they only pierce the barrier, like a farmer. The commentary pictures him at a full canal. He doesn't carry the water to his field in buckets. He cuts the little earth wall, and the water runs in by itself. Nature is already full. Your actions decide which wall gets cut. Nandi's devotion cut one. Nahusha's pride cut another. Here's the Hindu teaching, in the Upanishad's own plain words: as you act, as you live, so you become. Do good, become good; do harm, become harmful. That's karma, and the same Upanishad carries it into rebirth: what you're becoming doesn't stop at one body. Nahusha's story doesn't end in the dirt. Ages later, in the forest, the python seizes Bhima, and Yudhishthira answers its questions about who is truly a brahmin. Not birth, he says, but truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct, kindness. When the questions are answered, Nahusha is freed. Another wall cut. And Nandi is still at his post. In Shiva temples his image sits facing the shrine, and in many of them devotees stop at Nandi and whisper their prayers in his ear, because he's the one who never takes his eyes off Shiva. That's the farmer's lesson at both ends. You don't make the water. You choose the channel, and you turn into what you keep doing.

482.title: King Nriga's cow
482.hook: a king famous for giving away cows is found as a lizard in a well, and tells Krishna why
482.carry: good and bad both bind; offer the act
482.tomorrow: a sage, a fish, and an old desire
482.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer meals and work to God with words like Krishnarpanam astu, following the Gita's teaching (9.27–28) that action offered to God frees one from the bonds of good and bad results; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 4.7 alongside it.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nandi and Nahusha, one raised by devotion, one dropped by pride. As you act, so you become.
screen: `AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, some of Krishna's sons are out playing near Dvaraka and go looking for water. In a dry well they find a lizard, enormous, the size of a hill. They try ropes, they try leather straps; they can't lift it. So they run for their father. Krishna reaches down with his left hand and lifts it out, and at his touch the lizard becomes a shining man. Who are you? Krishna asks, though he knows. And the man says: I was a king. Nriga. Famous for giving.
screen: `A LIZARD THE SIZE OF A HILL.` → `KRISHNA LIFTS IT OUT.` → `I WAS A KING.`

segments.voice: Nriga had given away cows beyond counting, he says, as many as grains of sand, as stars. Then one day a cow he'd already given to one brahmin strayed back into his herd, and without knowing it, he gave her again, to another. The first man saw his cow being led away. The two argued it out before the king, and Nriga offered each a hundred thousand cows to let the other keep her. Both refused, and left angry. When Nriga died, Yama, judge of the dead, asked him: your good first, or your fault? He chose the fault first, and became the lizard in the well. Here's the teaching, and it surprises people. In Hindu thought, good karma doesn't cancel bad karma like a bank balance. Both ripen. Nriga got both. That's why, for Patanjali, even bright karma isn't the goal. Sutra 4.7: the action of the yogi is neither white nor black; for everyone else it's of three kinds, black, white and mixed. All three leave seeds. The fourth kind leaves none, because it's done without craving its fruit. The Gita names the way: whatever you do, eat, offer or give, do it as an offering to me, and you'll be freed from the bonds of good and bad results alike. So many Hindus finish a meal, or a day's work, with a quiet line: Krishnarpanam astu. Let this be offered to Krishna. The act still happens. The cows still get given. Nobody stands there waiting for the harvest.
screen: `ONE COW, GIVEN TWICE.` · `YOUR GOOD FIRST, OR YOUR FAULT?` · `BOTH RIPEN.` · `4.7: NEITHER WHITE NOR BLACK.` · `KRISHNARPANAM ASTU.` · then, large: `GOOD AND BAD BOTH BIND; OFFER THE ACT.`

483.title: Saubhari and the fish
483.hook: after years of austerity under the river, a sage watches a fish with its family, and an old desire wakes

483.howItsDone: Hindus speak of vasanas and samskaras carried from life to life in a samsara without beginning, and value satsang, the company of the good, in bhajan singing, temple gatherings and time with the wise; the Yoga Sutras teach removing what supports the traces rather than hunting for their origin.

screen: `GOOD AND BAD BOTH BIND; OFFER THE ACT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Saubhari spends years in austerity under the waters of the Yamuna, still as a stone. One day he watches a king of fish playing in the river with its mates and its little ones. Something stirs in the sage, a wish he thought was long gone: a family, a home, a life like that. So he climbs out and goes to King Mandhata, who has fifty daughters, and asks for one.
screen: `YEARS UNDER THE RIVER.` → `A FISH AND ITS FAMILY.` → `AN OLD WISH WAKES.`

segments.voice: The king looks at this thin old ascetic and stalls: my daughters choose for themselves. So Saubhari uses his yogic power to make himself young and handsome, and all fifty choose him. He builds them palaces and lives a life of every pleasure, and it never feels like enough. At last he sees it. A whole life of tapas, he says, and I fell because I kept company with a fish. One sight had woken a desire that was waiting all along. He gives it up, goes back to the forest, and the story says he found freedom. Patanjali gives the reason in two sutras. 4.10: the traces of desire, vasanas, have no beginning, because the wish to go on living is everlasting. You can't find the first craving; there isn't one. That's the Hindu teaching of samsara: the round of births has no starting point. But 4.11 turns the key. The traces are held up by four supports: a cause, a result, a place in the mind to rest, and an object to lean on. Take the supports away, and the traces go. Saubhari's object was a happy fish. His own advice afterward, in the Bhagavata: if you want freedom, stay out of company lost in pleasure, and keep company with great souls. Hindus call that satsang, the company of the good. It's why families sing bhajans together and sit with the wise. Not because the past can be erased, but because what you feed grows. So: no beginning, and still, an end.
screen: `FIFTY PALACES. NEVER ENOUGH.` · `I FELL BECAUSE OF A FISH.` · `4.10: NO FIRST CRAVING.` · `4.11: TAKE AWAY THE SUPPORTS.` · `SATSANG: THE COMPANY OF THE GOOD.` · then, large: `DESIRE HAS NO BEGINNING, BUT IT CAN END.`

segments.voice: Let a small want come up on its own: to check the phone, to shift, to get up. Don't ask where it started; ask what it's leaning on right now, a thought, a sound, an itch, and name it quietly. Then, if you pray, end with a few lines of a bhajan or a name of God you love: good company for the mind. If you don't, end with one line you trust.
Vasana, the trace desire leaves behind, like a scent left in cloth. These traces have no first moment, because the will to live has none, but they rest on supports, and without them they fall away.
